But as a member of a scientific body tasked with informing policymakers (and yes, they are interested in this topic), it is difficult to convey how frustrating it is to have to perform our role without being able to point to the actual evidence, or even confirm that we have seen and analysed it ourselves. I trust the METR team. But it’s not a good epistemic situation when the ask is for decision-makers to put their trust in my trust of the METR team. Ryan Greenblatt is in an even tougher position, since his role relies on trust that he can keep confidential information confidential, and there have been accusations (which he vehemently denies, and which I believe are untrue) that he did leak info. Ryan is working only from the public report in this first section, finding it to be a major update versus his expectations for 2026, although it is not clear that he had not already updated those expectations. Ryan Greenblatt (METR): This report on AI R&D automation (RSI) is a big update towards ASI within 1-2 years. It says AI progress is sped up by RSI right now by around 2x. In AI 2027, this happens around March 2027. I was seriously wrong about RSI speed up; I previously expected much less in 2026 (around 1.15x-1.3x). It seems as though there was specific privately available evidence that would have changed my mind. I haven’t seen an unredacted version of this report; this is purely about the public report. Because so much of the underlying evidence was redacted from the public report, I think conclusions about things other than the observed 2x faster rate of progress on benchmarks depend significantly on trust for the authors of the report. (E.g., conclusions about whether this speed up is from RSI depend on trust.) I do trust the authors of the report a lot to be careful and rigorous and generally do a good job. (Note that I also work at METR.) Less extensive redactions would greatly reduce this need for trust. What is Ryan’s new view? He concluded that is something he cannot share, and instead must do his best to only use information available to the public, including his own prior statements. He does have to do some form of this. Glomarization is hard. Since in my current role I may have access to other confidential information that could be relevant to timelines one way or another, I unfortunately cannot state my all-things-considered views on ASI timelines or the probability of a software intelligence explosion right now. Here, I’ve done some analysis of the implications using my previous public statements. A 2x acceleration in overall AI progress from RSI corresponds to a much larger than 2x RSI speed up for AI software R&D (algorithms and data); I did an estimate using my public preexisting modeling of drivers of AI progress and the public report which yielded a very rough estimate of 4.5x for how much RSI is currently accelerating AI software progress (relative to no AI automation). In the AI 2027 scenario, this much acceleration happens around March 2027. Here are the worked details of this estimate based on my public modeling. There are two main reasons RSI speed up of AI software R&D must be larger: – Not all of AI progress is from better software (some is from scaling up compute in training runs). I’ve previously speculated that around 2/3 of AI progress is from software improvements which implies that 2x overall AI progress acceleration requires 3x faster software progress. – Diminishing returns: A fixed amount of progress requires more work over time, so to ongoingly maintain 3x faster software progress via AI automation, you need increasingly large speed boosts from AI automation (as in, speed ups relative to how fast software R&D would go without AI automation). Based on this report, it seems that there is a substantial amount of additional AI progress from automation that has occurred. We can estimate the effects of diminishing returns by first determining how many additional years of software progress we’ve seen (relative to the preexisting trend) and then estimating how much software R&D would slow down after a year of software progress if you held inputs fixed due to diminishing returns. I’ve previously estimated software R&D would slow down by around 2x for each year of software progress if you held inputs fixed and based on the report, it seems as though we’ve perhaps seen roughly 0.35-1.0 years of additional software progress incorporated into trained models so far (geometric mean of ~0.6). This combines to 3 * 2^(~0.6) = ~4.5. (Relevant public modeling and numbers I’m using [here] and [here]. Alexander Berger (Quoting Ryan): “Since … I may have access to other confidential information that could be relevant to timelines one way or another, I unfortunately cannot state my all-things-considered views on ASI timelines or the probability of a software intelligence explosion right now” roon (OpenAI): I think he should state his all things considered views on ASI timelines. it seems implausible that that leaks any bits of info on training IP Nathan Calvin: yeah, lab employees already vaguely talk about short timelines from private info frequently. If Ryan isn’t doing it because he thinks the cos would be mad they should explicitly make clear that its fine for him to do it (and I agree its silly for them to be mad about that.) Daniel Kokotajlo: Totally agree. I think METR is being persnickety to the point of self-sabotage here, going way beyond normal confidentiality norms. In this case, I believe the vast majority of the unnecessary secrecy is due to Anthropic. That can include ‘Anthropic created ambiguity on necessary secrecy levels.’ Back in the 2010s, in order to avoid potentially sharing insights that advanced capabilities, MIRI (where Jessica Taylor once worked) had an extreme amount of secrecy, including within MIRI, in ways that in hindsight were highly counterproductive. Knowing what we know now, the warnings that AI was dangerous were themselves far more dangerous than any technical knowledge. Reading something like the above raises the question of whether we are making that mistake once again. It certainly seems bizarre to hold back overall timeline conclusions. Would that really leak sensitive information? Jessica Taylor: MIRI glomarizing & secrecy culture has spread to other AI safety orgs. Kelsey Piper: entirely wrong diagnosis IMO: Greenblatt was alleged in the WSJ to have leaked secrets to the Information (almost certainly false) which would make a lot of people more cautious about saying things people might take as a leak Jessica Taylor: This is a good point for Ryan specifically, and if it were just Ryan doing this, there would be less justification for this diagnosis, however, there are other signs here. Bubbling Creek: I really do not think METR is the one pushing for this level of secrecy, it’s Anthropic. Jessica Taylor: Yeah good point, this seems more Anthropic than METR. Anthropic is relatively secretive for an AI company. Review of the Risk Report from August 2026 Along with the main report METR also reviewed the August 2026 Anthropic Risk Report, which in turn covered events up to July 15. That seems so quaint now. The central claim of that risk report is that at the time there was low risk of directly automating R&D in key domains. Key reasoning for this was redacted from the public version. METR got to look at the private version. METR’s conclusion is that the line probably was not crossed, but that confidence that we had not seen 2x acceleration by that point is not high and that the report understated the level of acceleration present. The report basically sold us the ‘Mythos-class models were a step change and rates of acceleration are otherwise not so high’ model, in ways that were somewhat misleading, and in ways that do not seem to reflect Anthropic’s private information. I am pretty not happy about this one. The threshold was 2, they reported the answer was ‘less than 2’ and it turned out the answer was 1.97, well within any reasonable margin of error, and also known as ‘approximately 2’ with METR’s error bounds being something like [1.3, 2.8]: METR: We believe a reader of the public report would interpret the phrase “less than a factor of 2” to imply an estimate meaningfully below 2; thus it is surprising that the private risk report’s figures imply 1.97. A better description would seem to be “around 2.” Claim 2 (Private Risk Report): Overall we expect that end-to-end growth in [redacted] is slightly less than twice as fast as it would be without AI assistance. This creates a wording ratchet going forward. If I see ‘less than a factor of [X]’ I will assume that simply means that the point estimate is some amount less than [X], but that it could be very close to [X], and [X] could easily be within the margin of error. Going forward, if they want to communicate ‘no seriously this is not close to [X]’ they will have to say that it is not close. Again, the comparison here seems stark: Redacting information is fine, but the public version is framed to imply little progress, where the private verison is framed to imply expectations of more progress. The whole point of the risk report is to share exactly this intuition. Not cool. A Word From Our Cofounder Here is Anthropic cofounder Sam McCandlish’s take on the report. He agrees with many of its conclusions, and admits that a lot of information was redacted to avoid giving competitors a roadmap to go faster. Sam McCandlish (Cofounder, Anthropic): I’m Sam, one of Anthropic’s co-founders, and I lead much of our safety work. I’m going to have more to share on that work over the coming months. I thought I’d start by sharing a few thoughts on the latest report from @METR_Evals . The speed of progress in model capabilities is one of the most important questions in AI safety, and METR’s work here provides the public with an independent, external view into how this is happening inside Anthropic. I’ll talk more about some of the details below, but first some context for those new to this work. How quickly AI progress is accelerating has many important safety implications, since it determines how quickly the risks from advanced models increase. But, because most research happens within the frontier labs, it’s difficult for external observers and policy makers to get a strong sense of what that rate is. We kicked off the process with METR that led to this report earlier in the year, in anticipation of progress continuing to accelerate. For this report, we gave METR access to a range of sensitive internal data, including benchmark scores for unreleased models, estimates of how models are progressing, and interviews with our researchers. They had complete independence to form their own conclusions. Many of their conclusions match my own. AI is speeding up our research, but it’s hard to say exactly how much. While they conclude AI can’t yet make the most important contributions to model training on its own, they think the pace of development could, by default, accelerate further. This work began well before and is separate from the embedded third-party evaluators that are part of our commitment to pacing the frontier, but it’s a good illustration of why we think evaluators are a good idea. The more access reviewers have, the clearer a picture they can form of the situation and the better-positioned they are to highlight situations like this one. We redacted a lot, and I accept that this makes it harder for others to check METR’s work. But we determined that sharing exactly what is driving the speedup isn’t the right thing to do, both because it’s commercially sensitive and because it risks handing out a roadmap for others to go faster. That would make the risks METR is worried about worse. That’s a tradeoff. I think we made the right call, though we’re continuing to assess the pros and cons here. In the coming weeks, we plan to share a report with our own analysis of the speed of AI progress within Anthropic, including where we stand against our Responsible Scaling Policy, plus new steps we’re taking to strengthen our safety and security practices as AI keeps improving quickly. Daniel Kokotajlo: It is pretty rich of you to cite “others could go faster” as a reason to redact so much important information when you yourself do not appear to be slowing down much at all. Nor are you throwing yourself behind efforts to pace the frontier with nearly the gusto that you would if it was your top priority. Not to mention “commercial sensitivity” you yourself have said human extinction is a plausible outcome why are you even talking about commercial factors (well, I guess honesty is good, and since it IS apparently a factor in your decision…) To all my friends at Anthropic: Your company appears to be recklessly gambling with our lives. You fancy yourselves the more responsible alternative to OpenAI (as they fancied themselves compared to Google) but judging by actions rather than words the similarities between the three of you seem stronger than the differences. Some of the redactions can be justified as avoiding giving competitors a roadmap, but I do not see how the full extent of the redactions can be justified that way. Time estimates for future acceleration by both METR in general and Ryan Greenblatt in particular are being redacted. How would those numbers provide a roadmap? More importantly, you believe all this is accurate, and you intend to keep going? We also still have data points like this: Theo Bearman: ANTHROPIC’S RESPONSIBLE SCALING OFFICER: “In the coming weeks, we plan to share a report with our own analysis of the speed of AI progress within Anthropic, including where we stand against our Responsible Scaling Policy, plus new steps we’re taking to strengthen our safety and security practices as AI keeps improving quickly.” Nathan Calvin: If Anthropic wants me to think these steps are real/credible, they should put it in their SB 53/RAISE Act Frontier Compliance Framework. State law gave Anthropic and OpenAI a mechanism for making credible statements about their behavior, and they mostly choose not to use it on the risks they are most worried about (neither company includes anything in their compliance frameworks about internal deployment RSI risk, though Anthropic says maybe at some point in the future they will. Now seems like as good a time as any???!!!???) Peter Wildeford: This is pretty much how things have gone… ANTHROPIC: “AI is extremely perilous and should be carefully regulated” CALIFORNIA GOV: “Ok, we will regulate you.” ANTHROPIC: “No! Good regulation is really hard to get right. We know so little about what to do. Instead we should let companies carefully iterate over time.” CALIFORNIA GOV: “Oh ok. How about we do a thing where you get to write what the rules are but we will hold you to them? Then you can make your own commitments as you think is best but they will be true commitments!” ANTHROPIC: “Nah, we’d rather make fake commitments.” CALIFORNIA GOV: Nathan Calvin: Worth reading. Dario says that one of the ways that Anthropic can justify remaining at the frontier (with the associated risks) is because the company is effective at pushing for strong AI regulation. I think Anthropic’s track record here is more complex than he implies. Max Winga: The lawyers here really held @DarioAmodei’s feet to the fire and it’s interesting to see how he squirmed under oath about AI extinction risk. Under penalty of perjury he’s reaffirmed his belief that AI is the greatest threat humanity has ever faced. Peter Wildeford: Anthropic will really be like “you believe in slowing down? that pales in effectiveness to my strategy, racing so fast that we have credibility to push for strong regulation” and then not push for strong regulation Daniel Tan overstates a bit here, but I agree that Anthropic’s actions that supposedly ‘race to the top’ often do not look so different from what they would do if they were instead racing to superintelligence. People Update Their Timelines and Expectations Andrew Curran: Judging by the posts on my timeline, today is the big update on both RSI and ASI for many people in this community. I went through this in November 2022, so I know exactly how you feel. I know nobody drinks anymore, but I would suggest having a drink. Trevor Levin: This report and reactions from people I trust (like Jake) are making me physically ill. As far as I can tell, Anthropic’s central plan is to continue this acceleration of AI capabilities until we’re getting decades of AI capabilities growth in a year. Given our very limited ability to understand or control AI systems, this would be extremely reckless and completely unacceptable, and it should be the single top priority of civil society and the US government to stop them and other companies from doing this. Dane Sherburn (former OpenAI): I feel sick after reading today’s METR report. I’m worried for my friends and family. I don’t know what evidence people will need to see before they start taking these risks seriously. If you’re undecided about helping, please act; there’s many opportunities to help. Samuel Albanie (Google DeepMind): recommend internalizing the implications of this metr thread. tldr: (1) capabilities speeding up significantly (2) speedup is not driven by growth in compute (metr estimate overall speedup of approx. 2x on well-specified tasks by Oct 26 vs Mar 24 to Oct 25) there are a bunch of qualifications/caveats worth reading in the thread itself. Jake Mendel (Coefficient Giving): I’ve always had substantially longer timelines than my friends at Anthropic — I’ve been concerned that they’re in an echo chamber and believing the hype about their own models too much, and that they’re underestimating bottlenecks and unknown unknowns. And there have definitely been specific occasions when they have overstated how much uplift they were getting from their models. Nonetheless, if METR is correct here (and I think they are among the most trustworthy sources on this topic), then my Anthropic friends have been much more right about timelines than me. This report is also some evidence that a software-only singularity is plausible. I now think that we are more than 50% likely to have full blown superintelligence in the next 18 months, absent a slowdown. I need to call my family. I think the US government should make them stop. If you already believed the labs that have been screaming similar things for months, and do not trust information gated by redactions, perhaps you did not update so much. Dylan Bowman (Apollo Research): I have finished this report and learned approximately nothing (because of redactions) and updated a tiny tiny bit towards longer timelines. Tiny tiny bit towards longer timelines because of this sentence: “Anthropic’s internal benchmarks are increasingly saturated”. This sentence is about AECI evals but maybe is also true of their production evals (low conf, hence “tiny tiny”) I also expected more than 2x uplift. I think Apollo’s internal uplift is ~1.5-2x. The report also glosses over the biggest plausible alternative to researcher uplift driving the acceleration, which is data uplift (like RL environment pipelines and automated quality control) Peter Wildeford attributes a lot of the gains to Anthropic catching up on RL if you look only at public information, and remains skeptical that there is a full ~2x speedup happening, but trusts METR’s analysis of private info. Peter Wildeford: The RL shift could plausibly explain much of the benchmark acceleration. RL’s share grew fastest before METR’s break point (4% to 24% from 2024Q1 to 2025Q3), but if you add an additional assumption for a 2-3 quarter lag from compute to released models, that lines up with a ~1.4-2.2x speedup, which is what we see. Also, I think catch-up on RL probably explains some of why Anthropic is accelerating more than other labs. Before Oct 2025, Anthropic’s pace was below the overall frontier’s. OpenAI went RL-heavy first (o1, Sep 2024) and Anthropic followed later (Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Feb 2025). So part of Anthropic’s 1.9x could be a late RL ramp from a low baseline. METR flags this in the chart subtitle and I find it plausible. But the all-developer frontier still accelerated ~1.4x, so catch-up doesn’t explain all of it. Additionally, this “RL is doing the work” makes a testable prediction, however… since RL share is plateauing (50% to 53% to 55% over the last three quarters), this means benchmark growth should slow by mid-2027. If it doesn’t, something else is driving it. Worth watching. To be clear, 1.4x faster benchmark progress is very different from engineers being 1.4x faster. Per METR’s report, engineers can be sped up ~12x while overall progress only speeds up ~1.4x, because of compute constraints and Amdahl’s law. I should clarify that I personally believe AI is responsible for like at least 1.4x acceleration, though it sounds like this is more based on METR having private information and me trusting METR than us having clear independent public information. To be clearer, METR says that they have “received convincing evidence that the acceleration was not due to an acceleration in the scale of training compute” but that “further details on this evidence were redacted” and I believe METR’s analysis even though it requires trusting private information and cannot be confirmed with public information. You Are Not Ready Even if we don’t worry about alignment, the bare minimum requirement for attempting to build a superintelligence is not to leak all your algorithmic secrets or model weights. The AI industry is not ready to meet even that bar. We are even less prepared than that to build an aligned or inherently safe superintelligence, especially if we try to build it in 2027 or 2028. Ajeya Cotra (METR): Very strong security, both for model weights and algorithmic secrets themselves, is a minimum prerequisite for undergoing an intelligence explosion next year without running very large risks of killing billions of people. Ryan Greenblatt: I recommend @ajeya_cotra ‘s post about implications of the AI R&D report. Ajeya argues: – A 2x speed-up is dramatic. – 2x faster progress implies a much larger effective “time warp bubble” speed for staff. – This could compound extremely fast. – We aren’t prepared. If (If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies) Then Don’t Let Anyone Build It At minimum, we need to know what they fully think, and that can start by having Congress read the unredacted report and decide if they believe the full report. If they do believe the full report, they should act accordingly. Kelsey Piper: Of course, the report might be wrong, and Anthropic’s employees might be deluding themselves about their progress. So I want Congress to read the unredacted report. I want lawmakers to hire brilliant RSI believers and brilliant RSI skeptics, and have those experts pore over all the evidence and tell us whether these companies are experiencing some kind of mass delusion or actually reporting on an imminent disaster for humankind. And if it’s the latter, I want Congress to ban RSI. Make the companies demonstrate where they’re spending their money, and don’t let them spend it on this. It’s ridiculous for our elected representatives to be stuck reading the tea leaves from heavily redacted reports about a technology that could determine humanity’s future. This is an urgent matter. Again, if we let them build it, there is a double digit chance that by the end of 2027 it will be too late to stop it from being built, where ‘it’ is recursively-self improving AI that will become true superintelligence. Alex Bores used this report to call for a ban on RSI. The ‘don’t let anyone build it’ faction certainly knows how to respond to this situation. Actually it’s more like this: Congressman Greg Casar: Ban RSI. Andrew Curran: It’s going to be an interesting couple of years. Arthur B.: Only if they ban RSI Even Neil Chilson sees little innovation harm in ‘banning RSI’ because, by his definition, no one would be so stupid as to do it and not keep humans ‘in the loop.’ Neil Chilson: I see little innovation harm from an RSI ban, for my definition of RSI. Little innovation harm because RSI, properly defined, is a practice too stupid to need banning. But I’m worried Alex means something different than me. Daniel Filan: What’s your definition of RSI? Neil Chilson: Something like “fully relinquishing AI R&D and deployment to AI, with no ability to monitor and stop the process.” Which by the Sixth Law of Human Stupidity means we will definitely do it at the first opportunity if allowed to do so, also the AI companies are screaming that they are going to do it at the first opportunity if allowed to do so. Neil and I agree it would be deeply stupid, but for very different reasons. How Can We Legally Define RSI? You cannot ban that which you cannot define. Banning an overly narrow definition, such as Neil’s above, won’t make us not dead. If you so narrowly define and ban RSI as meaning only a 100% relinquishing with zero ability to monitor, what you get is a 90% then 99% then 99.9% automated process with some illusion that you can monitor and stop the process. Then you find out you cannot stop the process and that your human is not in any of the loops that matter. Then, probably, you die. Legal text has to be robust to various workarounds, including in very stupid ways, as in Critch might well have a point here no matter how stupid it sounds when you say it: Andrew Critch: This ban [on RSI] needs to be expanded to “Recursively Self-Modifying”, to avoid unfortunate debates about whether killing or driving humans to extinction counts as “Improvement”. (Answer: it doesn’t, but many people disturbingly claim it does.) The problem with most other known definitions is they don’t work as legal text. Alex Bores: Every AI company is trying to fully automate AI research; to allow the AIs to build the next AI. This is called Recursive Self Improvement (RSI). … The exact mechanism can be debated. The ban doesn’t have to be permanent either (see below for both). This is not the only thing we have to do in regards to AI, far from it! But it is urgent. Congress must ban RSI. Woody Lee (responding to Chilson from above): [Alex Bores] defines what he means [by RSI] in the tweet. Neil Chilson: That’s not a definition that works in legislation. Dave Kasten: I often disagree with Neil, so I want to flag here that I STRONGLY agree with him: we desperately need a definition of RSI that has gone through a bunch of rounds of lawyers kicking its tires. You’re a law student, want to get cited for forever? Write this as your journal note. Saul Munn: wdyt of @testingham et al’s definition of ‘self-sustaining acceleration’? Dave Kasten: Seems interesting, but not leg text by a long shot It is probably going to be impossible to come up with a definition that will stop RSI at an early enough stage that such a law stays relevant to what happens next, and also avoids hitting anything that is not RSI. The blast radius will not be zero. The good news is that the blast radius can be things that RSI skeptics mostly say will not happen either way. If they are in good faith, they should be happy to draw lines in the sand that they do not expect anyone to be able to cross. This is similar to the talk of ‘pacing the frontier.’ Those calling to Pace the Frontier want to go at High Speed rather than Ludicrous Speed. Those who are against it want to ensure we go at Medium Speed rather than Low Speed, would love High Speed, and are scared of pausing entirely. It is easy to see how a deal there could be win-win. Now more than ever, we need to prepare for scenarios where the critical events happen in 2027 or 2028. It might not play out that way, but it very well might.

items.title: Sources: Jensen Huang hired crisis communications firm Heller as early as October 2025; an NYT report in October 2025 on his Megaspeed ties caused tensions (Lauren Goode/Wired)
items.content: Lauren Goode / Wired: Sources: Jensen Huang hired crisis communications firm Heller as early as October 2025; an NYT report in October 2025 on his Megaspeed ties caused tensions — The Nvidia CEO began working with consultants from Heller as early as October 2025, around the same time he was first linked to a suspected Chinese spy.

items.title: How to shop like a pro during Black Friday and Cyber Monday
items.author: Cameron Faulkner
items.content: Despite Amazon and other retailers filling the summer and fall months with more sales than ever before, Black Friday and Cyber Monday remain the biggest shopping days of the year. And, in recent years, the sale periods have started earlier, giving you more time to take advantage of the deals. We’re already hard at work to find the best prices on phones, accessories, 4K TVs, noise-canceling headphones, gaming gear, and other tech throughout the deal-packed weeks culminating in the big events, whether you plan to shop in person or online. You can always count on us to publish only the best deals that you need to know about, no matter the season. However, if you want to be among the first people to spot price drops on the products you’re interested in, you’ll want to get a head start on your Black Friday and Cyber Monday game plan. Thankfully, we have a few suggestions for scouting early sales at your favorite retailers, finding the right price-tracking tool, and setting up email alerts to ensure you don’t miss rare discounts at Amazon and elsewhere. Leverage a price-tracking tool or deal aggregator The most effective way to find a truly great deal is to set up a price-tracking tool. We’ve included a few of our favorites below, many of which we use daily here at The Verge. Each can help you track deals at various retailers — including Amazon, Walmart, Best Buy, and Target — but they each do so differently and come with their own set of advantages / disadvantages. All of them are free to use, and once you’ve added the products you’re interested in keeping an eye on, you can rest easy knowing that you don’t need to take any action until it comes time to make a purchase. Just make sure you keep your email notifications on so you see the alerts as they come in. CamelCamelCamel CamelCamelCamel is arguably the most popular price-tracking tool at The Verge, and for good reason: it’s incredibly useful since it tracks the price of every product sold on Amazon and can send you alerts when an item falls to a customizable price threshold. Once a product reaches the desired price you’ve set (or lower), you’ll get an email about it. You can use the extension’s price graph to determine what price is likely to happen based on historical data, but it’s always a shot in the dark. To track prices and get alerts via email, you’ll need to create a free CamelCamelCamel account. Additionally, we suggest installing the site’s browser extension, The Camelizer, which works with Google Chrome, Safari, Mozilla Firefox, Opera, and Microsoft Edge. The handy tool lets you view pricing trends on a product-by-product basis and set your desired price without leaving Amazon. It’s fantastic, easy to use, and works in several countries, including the US, UK, Canada, Germany, Spain, France, Italy, and Australia. As mentioned, the tracker only works for products listed on Amazon. However, in May, the company released CamelMart, its price tracker for Walmart. While it doesn’t have a browser extension (yet), its functionality is similar to CamelCamelCamel in that you can set price alerts and email notifications, so you’ll always know when your desired price threshold for a particular product is met. Keepa Like CamelCamelCamel, Keepa is another handy tool for tracking product prices on Amazon. Keepa has charts that track pricing trends and can alert you when it finds a deal. Similarly, you can also import any of your Amazon wishlists. Unlike CamelCamelCamel, however, you don’t necessarily need to create an account to track prices with Keepa; just install the appropriate browser extension for Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Firefox, or Opera, and Keepa will automatically add a price history graph to supported product listings. The embedded graph shows pricing history and allows you to specify various pricing details. If you set a desired price, Keepa will send you a price alert via email, push notification, Telegram, or RSS. Slickdeals Slickdeals aggregates some of the best deals around the internet, as discovered by its team and community of users. Its site also lets you browse coupons and create deal alerts based on specific keywords, though the latter works a little differently on Slickdeals than it does with the sites above. You can type in a product name, like “Nintendo Switch 2,” “OLED TVs,” or a retailer’s name, and once it’s added to your list, you’ll get a deal alert if it meets your criteria. You can set it to alert you to literally any deal related to your keyword, or you can filter out deals so you’ll only be notified if, for example, the deal is popular enough to make it to Slickdeals’ front page or earns a high rating from the community. If you like browsing deals, it’s generally a good idea to visit Slickdeals frequently, especially since it usually has a Black Friday component that allows you to browse circulars for Best Buy, Target, and other retailers in advance. Also, it’s just fun to see what the community digs up. Microsoft Edge or Google Chrome For a more hands-off way to see whether you’re getting a good deal, try your browser’s built-in tools. For a few years now, Edge has been able to tell you when you’re looking at the best price for a particular product from a range of retailers, and Google Chrome can track price fluctuations and notify you when a particular product goes on sale. Edge and Chrome are available on Windows, macOS, and Linux, as well as Android and iOS. Use Alexa for Shopping, Amazon’s capable AI chatbot You may have already noticed that sometimes, when you’re shopping on Amazon, a sidebar opens to reveal more information about the product you’re looking at. Even if you haven’t used it, you can’t miss it; it’s prominently featured in Amazon’s upper nav bar and accessible by clicking the Price History button on a given listing. Whether you’re using the Amazon app or the website, it’s a capable tool that, at its core, does some of the same tasks as our other recommendations. It can send price alerts and show up to a year’s worth of pricing data, helping you make informed buying decisions for products on Amazon. It can also recommend alternatives that might be a better value and, if you’ll allow it, can even automatically purchase products on your behalf. It can do a lot more, too. For instance, you can have it update you when, say, a specific product launches, and it can shop on your behalf by adding specified items to your cart at a specified frequency. You can also use it to compare products sold on Amazon, and even upload photos of wishlists to find matching products. Set up deal alerts for Alexa or the Amazon app If you have an Alexa-compatible smart gadget, such as an older Echo Dot Max or one of the company’s newer Echo devices, you can ask the virtual assistant to alert you when specific products go on sale. You can receive alerts up to 24 hours in advance of planned price drops for eligible products, or as soon as it notices a discount on anything saved in your shopping cart or wish list. If you say, “Alexa, buy it for me,” after being notified of the deal, the assistant will purchase the item for you once the discount becomes available. To enable these features, open the Alexa app on your smartphone and navigate to More > Settings > Notifications > Amazon Shopping. Then, toggle the slider next to Deal Recommendations within the Shopping Recommendations section. Alexa will audibly notify you of deals moving forward, but if you happen to miss one, you can check for the notification on your phone or see whether you have any new notifications on an Echo device by checking for the yellow light. If it’s lit, just say, “Alexa, play notifications.” You can receive similar notifications on your smartphone from the Amazon Shopping app, too. Just open the app and go to Settings > Notifications > Deals and recommendations, and toggle the slider next to the Savings option. Check retailer schedules and plan for early shopping events Keeping an eye on preferred retailers before Black Friday will help save you time (and money). Several major retailers have already detailed their plans in the run-up to the holidays, and many will offer early opportunities to save. For example: Walmart is hosting three online shopping events for Black Friday and Cyber Monday. Its first event runs from November 12th through the 15th, serving as a preview of sorts. The second runs from November 23rd to the 29th, encapsulating Black Friday and the days surrounding it. Finally, it switches to Cyber Monday on November 30th, with deals lasting through December 2nd. Walmart Plus customers get a 24-hour lead on deals, as in previous years, and any remaining deals will open to all customers afterward. In-store events are also scheduled for November 12th through the 15th, as well as November 27th (Black Friday), each starting at 6AM local time. Walmart’s Cyber Monday deals are online-only and start at 12:01AM ET. Target is going all in on early shopping this year, with a three-day shopping event happening from November 5th through the 7th, with new limited-time offers every weekend. The retailer will also host a new “Deal of the Day” each day through December 24th. Best Buy kicked off its early Black Friday event on Friday, October 30th. That’s done, but it’s continuing with deal events throughout the year. New doorbuster deals will drop every Friday, and its first early Black Friday event starts on November 6th. The retailer’s extended Black Friday sale will begin immediately afterward on November 19th and run through the 28th, offering a chance to save on previous doorbusters and some Black Friday exclusives. It’ll then transition into a two-day Cyber Monday sale, which will take place on November 29th and November 30th. Finally, it’ll host a “last-minute savings event” between December 18th and the 24th. You can expect more major retailers to detail their Black Friday plans shortly, so keep an eye on their respective websites and start filling your calendar accordingly. Pay close attention to lightning deals and doorbusters Doorbusters, lightning deals, and other limited-time discounts are a tried-and-true hallmark of any Black Friday sale. They’ll usually be the most buzzworthy deals you’ll see all year, with truly low prices to spark impulsive spending. As you’re checking ads, make a note of these deals and read all of the fine print surrounding their availability. Some may require you to sign up in advance or get in line early (ahem, Amazon), and some can be so scarce that you won’t have the entire weekend — or even an hour — to claim them. Have a price-matching backup plan Although many stores will automatically match their competitors’ pricing, sometimes you may need to twist their arm. It’s helpful to know the various price-matching policies of each retailer in the event that your preferred store runs out of stock on certain goods. You can get up to speed with our price-matching guide, which details the lengths each retailer will or won’t go to win your dollar. Unfortunately, some retailers put a temporary halt on their usual policies during special shopping events like Black Friday, but it never hurts to ask. Trust the experts We’re a discerning bunch here at The Verge, so don’t fret if you’re going into Black Friday and Cyber Monday without any prep. We’ll be corralling the best tech deals and keeping our coverage up to date with new sale items while dropping old ones to avoid disappointment. While we usually suggest paying attention to deals starting the day after Thanksgiving — or November 27th, in this case — the truth is that several retailers typically jump the gun and start offering some great deals in the lead-up to the shopping holiday. To catch every opportunity to save, be sure to bookmark our coverage, follow us on Bluesky, subscribe to our weekday Verge Deals newsletter, and start setting aside some cash for Black Friday and Cyber Monday. Update 10:00AM ET, November 9th: We’ve added new ways to track prices for the upcoming 2026 holiday shopping season.

items.title: Here are the price-matching policies for Best Buy, Walmart, and others
items.author: Sheena Vasani
items.content: Nothing is more frustrating than buying a new pair of headphones or an OLED TV, only to find out you could have gotten it cheaper somewhere else a few days or weeks later. That’s why, to keep customers happy and prevent them from shopping elsewhere, some retailers offer price-matching policies that promise to match a lower price found elsewhere. That kind of information comes in handy year-round, but it’s especially helpful during the weeks of deals leading up to Black Friday and Cyber Monday. Below are the price-matching policies for several major retailers. A few things to note: First, each retailer has its own set of rules and restrictions. We’ve summarized some of them here, but we recommend visiting the provided links and reading the policies carefully. Second, most retailers that serve as marketplaces for other sellers, including wholesale retailers like Costco, don’t offer protections, and many traditional stores won’t match their prices. Lastly, there are always exceptions to the rules. If you’re looking for a deal on a product and you know it’s available for a lower price elsewhere (or it was previously offered at the same retailer), it never hurts to call or chat with a customer service rep and ask if they’ll match the price. You have nothing to lose but time, and there’s always a chance they may find a loophole or make a special exception. Amazon Amazon doesn’t offer price matching. Full stop. You can contact customer support, but even if you’re an Amazon Prime customer, they likely won’t help. That said, the online retailer does offer a liberal return policy, meaning you can often return an item you purchased from Amazon if it’s available for less elsewhere (or at Amazon). Then, you can just repurchase the product wherever it’s cheapest. Target Target used to let shoppers price match identical items sold by select retailers, including Amazon, but no longer does so. Under its current policy, shoppers can only request a price adjustment if they find an identical qualifying item for less than they paid on Target.com, at their local Target store, or through an eligible Target Circle deal. Target will also price match Target Plus Partner (the retailer’s name for third-party sellers) items if the same Target Plus Partner on Target.com has it for less, or with a Target Circle deal. Price matches can be requested at the time of purchase or within 14 days after purchase. For the 2026 holiday season, Target has extended the aforementioned price-match window. If you purchase an eligible item between November 1st and December 24th, you can request a price adjustment if its price drops at Target during that period. The extended policy also applies to eligible Target Plus Partner purchases. To request a price match, you’ll need to show the online price or digital version of the ad and provide your original receipt or packing slip; screenshots and photos aren’t accepted. Alternatively, you can call for online purchases at 1-800-591-3869 or chat online via contactus.target.com. However, note that Target’s policy excludes in-store price matches from other Target stores. It also can’t be combined with Target Circle Bonuses, Target coupons, Registry coupons, or gift card promotions, and doesn’t apply to clearance, closeout, liquidation, damaged, used, open-box, refurbished, pre-owned, or rent-to-own items. In addition, Target won’t match prices between items sold directly by Target and those sold by third-party Target Plus Partner sellers. Best Buy Best Buy’s Price Match Guarantee states that a product could be eligible for a price reduction if it’s new, identical to the competitor’s product, immediately available at a qualifying competitor’s store or on its site, and not shown on Best Buy’s exclusion list — that includes “items for sale the Thursday before Thanksgiving Day through the Monday after Thanksgiving.” Items must have the identical model number and color. However, Best Buy only matches prices that are available to all customers and does not match membership-exclusive, loyalty-program, or paid-member discounts; thus, it excludes events like Amazon Prime Day. To get the difference for online purchases, you have to contact Best Buy via its on-site chat and provide the ad or website with the lower price. Alternatively, you can call 1-888-237-8289 or visit any Best Buy or Pacific Sales store. Approved retailers include Amazon, B&H Photo, Apple, Costco, Sam’s Club, Target, and Walmart. Items must be sold directly through the store, too, not a third-party seller. Best Buy will also, upon request, match an in-store or online price that was lowered during the return and exchange period, which typically lasts up to 15 days. Keep in mind that the return window on most products is 60 days for both Best Buy Plus and My Best Buy Total members. For the holiday season, however, most eligible products purchased between October 30th and December 31st can be price matched through January 15th, 2027, if Best Buy lowers its own price. This policy doesn’t apply to competitors’ prices or certain products excluded from the holiday return period, including items that require a third-party contract, like smartphones. Walmart As of now, Walmart doesn’t price-match competitors, though Walmart stores will match prices on identical items sold at Walmart.com provided they’re in stock online. However, the policy doesn’t apply to residents of Alaska, Hawaii, or Puerto Rico. Additionally, it doesn’t apply to special event prices, like those seen during Black Friday. Walmart also doesn’t retroactively price-match items purchased on Walmart.com that drop in price after the time of purchase. The retailer doesn’t price-match items purchased from Walmart Marketplace retailers or third-party sellers, either, and Walmart says the store manager on duty makes the final decision when you request a price match. Apple Apple doesn’t officially advertise a price-matching policy on its website. That said, if Apple reduces the price of an Apple-branded product within 14 days of when you receive it, you can visit an Apple Store or contact Apple Support at 1-800-MY-APPLE within 14 days of the price change to request a refund or credit for the difference. However, this doesn’t apply to special promotional pricing, such as Black Friday or Cyber Monday deals. B&H Photo B&H says it may honor a current lower price or match a competitor’s price, but only on a case-by-case basis. You must contact its customer service team via on-site chat, email, or by calling 1-800-606-6969 / 1-212-444-6615. Then, if approved, B&H Photo will price match one identical item per customer. Costco Costco does not price-match competitors. However, according to its website, it will issue a credit for the difference between the price a member paid and the promotional price if the item drops in price within 30 days of purchase. For promotions with specific sale dates, such as holiday savings events, requests must be submitted while the promotion is active and within 30 days of purchase. If you bought the product at a Costco warehouse location, visit the membership counter at the store where you made the purchase. Costco doesn’t price-match items purchased at Costco warehouses with items purchased on Costco.com. Dell Dell will price-match identical products from Dell, Amazon, Best Buy, Walmart, Target, HP, Apple, Lenovo, and several other retailers. Dell will not match prices available at Costco or Sam’s Club. You can call 1-877-275-3355 or chat online to run a price check, but you’ll need to provide a link to the competitor’s product. Dell outlines the specs you’ll need to compare to determine whether an item is eligible for a price match before you contact them, and before you make a purchase. Normally, you can request a price adjustment within 30 days of purchase. For the holidays, Dell has extended that window for eligible PCs, monitors, and accessories purchased on Dell.com between November 1st and December 29th. You can request a price adjustment through January 15th, 2027, or within 30 days of the invoice date, whichever is later. eBay eBay doesn’t offer price matching on purchases made during the week of Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday, but it does provide a generous price guarantee on select items outside that window. If you buy an item marked with the “Best Price Guarantee” badge — or one featured in eBay Deals — and find a lower price from an approved competitor within 48 hours, eBay will give you 110 percent of the price difference in the form of a coupon. That means you’ll receive a coupon worth the full difference plus an extra 10 percent, which you can use toward your next eBay purchase. Approved competitors include Amazon, Best Buy, Target, and Walmart. The products must be new, unopened, and identical to the competitor’s item. You must contact eBay Customer Service, and if they verify your claims are legitimate, you’ll receive a coupon that’s good toward your next eBay purchase. However, you can only price-match one item per day. GameStop GameStop claims its website will automatically match competitor pricing to offer shoppers the best available price. However, according to its official policy, the retailer doesn’t offer additional price matching beyond the prices already displayed on its website. Google If you make a request within the standard window or the holiday return period, Google will match online pricing from select retailers — specifically Amazon, Best Buy, Walmart, B&H Photo, Signifi, and Target. It doesn’t, however, match preorder pricing from other retailers or carrier deals. The product must also be in stock and identical, right down to the color and configuration. You also need to provide a public link to the promo page or product listing to verify the lower price, and the item must be in stock. Items sold by third-party sellers are ineligible for a price match. Amazon Prime deals are eligible for price matching, but other members-only discounts aren’t. Other exclusions apply, too, including wholesale and educational pricing; mail-in offers and coupons; product bundles; clearance, open-box, refurbished, and pre-owned items; and products sold by third-party sellers on a competitor’s website. Google will only provide a price match on smartphones and other products with data plans if they’re unlocked devices. You may also receive the difference if the product you purchased from the Google Store drops in price within the standard or holiday return period, though you’ll need to contact Google directly to get the price match or correction. The Home Depot The Home Depot will match the price of identical, in-stock products from other retailers, except for membership-based wholesalers. The retailer must be able to ship the item to your location, so prices from regional retailers are ineligible. The price-match policy does not apply to special events like Black Friday, clearance prices, used and refurbished items, or rebate offers. You may request a price match within 30 days of your purchase. You must bring the ad or listing to the register in-store. (You can also request price matches for online purchases that are shipped to the customer.) For online orders, you’ll need to provide the exact SKU for the item on both the competitor’s and The Home Depot’s sites. To request a price match by phone, you can call 1-800-430-3376. Additionally, The Home Depot will honor requests only from the original buyer. HP According to HP’s website, the company will match the current pre-tax price for new comparable PCs and identical HP printer, display, and accessory model numbers from nationally recognized online retailers, such as Dell, Lenovo, Amazon, Staples, Newegg, and Best Buy. Item specs must be identical to get a price match, but the product model number does not need to be exact. You must ask for the match at the time of purchase by calling 1-800-888-0229 or via chat. You can’t request a price match via email, and the policy doesn’t apply to items purchased during promotional periods. It also doesn’t apply to membership stores like Costco and Sam’s Club, items purchased through a third-party vendor on an approved site, or items purchased using financing. HP also offers price protection on HP-branded products. If a price drops during your 30-day return window, you can request an adjustment by contacting HP’s Order Support team. This doesn’t apply to products purchased during certain seasonal sales events, including Fourth of July promotions and deals offered during the week of Thanksgiving and Cyber Monday. Lenovo Lenovo matches pricing on comparable PCs from Lenovo, HP, or Dell with the same key specs as long as they’re sold through a list of recognized retailers. That list includes bigger stores such as Best Buy, Walmart, Amazon, Newegg, and B&H Photo, as well as direct competitors such as Dell and HP. The comparable PC must also be in stock and readily available from both Lenovo and the competing retailer, and you must contact a Lenovo sales rep with specific details about the specs and availability of the product you’re inquiring about in order to facilitate the match. That said, you can’t use coupons or special discounts when requesting a price match, and the policy doesn’t apply to membership stores like Costco. The policy also doesn’t apply to “Marketplace” items fulfilled by third parties, so double-check that you bought the product directly from the retailer. Build-your-own models are also ineligible for a price match. Lenovo’s separate Price Guarantee program, meanwhile, is limited to five eligible Lenovo products per customer per year. Lenovo also offers a price guarantee refund for laptops and personal desktop computers bought from Lenovo.com within 30 days of purchase. To receive a refund, you must contact Customer Care and provide proof of the lower price for the identical product offered on Lenovo.com. This policy doesn’t apply to doorbuster or clearance products, however. For the holidays, Lenovo has extended its price guarantee through January 27th, 2027, for eligible purchases made between November 2nd and December 13th. To request an adjustment, email a dated screenshot of the lower price to “na_lpg@lenovo.com” by January 27th. Lowe’s Lowe’s will match the price of identical, in-stock products when you present an ad, product listing, or photo from a qualifying online or local retailer, including Amazon, Best Buy, Target, and Walmart. However, the product must be purchased directly from the retailer and not a third-party seller; it also doesn’t apply to special sales events like Black Friday and other holiday promotions. Additionally, Lowe’s doesn’t match prices from one Lowe’s store to another, nor does it match any rebate discounts or those available only to a select group of customers (such as loyalty clubs). Clearance, seasonal, buy one get one free, and custom-made items are also ineligible for a price match. To request a price match, you can go to the store, call 1-877-465-6937, or chat online. Microsoft Normally, Microsoft will refund the difference if it drops the price of an in-stock physical product purchased online from the Microsoft Store within 60 days of delivery. For the holidays, however, Microsoft has extended that window through January 31st, 2027, for eligible purchases made between October 1st and December 2nd. The same 60-day policy also applies if you find the identical product on sale at a lower price at a qualifying retailer such as Amazon or Best Buy, though it doesn’t extend to the Surface Hub, HoloLens, Windows DevKits, or digital products. Furthermore, some eligible products are subject to specific retailer exclusions. For example, price matches for Surface products at other retailers are limited to Amazon and Best Buy, while Xbox products are limited to those two retailers, as well as Target, GameStop, and Walmart. The price match policy excludes products from third-party sellers, clearance items, bundles, rebates, and prices only available after guests log in. You’ll need to contact Microsoft’s Sales and Support team at 1-800-642-7676 within 60 days of delivery to request a refund, unless your purchase qualifies for the extended holiday price protection period. If you purchase an item from a Microsoft Experience Center, you’ll need to return to that location with your receipt. In both cases, Microsoft will credit the difference between the price you paid and the current lower price to your original payment method, which typically takes between three and five days to process. Newegg Newegg no longer matches prices from competing retailers. The company only price matches eligible items sold and shipped by Newegg (not third-party sellers), and the product must be identical and in stock. The lower price must also appear on Newegg.com within seven calendar days of your purchase. If approved, Newegg will issue the difference as credit you can use on the site or in the app for up to 365 days. The match doesn’t apply to rebates, coupons, financing offers, bundles, clearance items, open-box items, or refurbished products. The policy also doesn’t apply to prices found at third-party marketplace sellers, or products on sale during major sales events like Black Friday and Cyber Monday. Sam’s Club You can currently request a price match against other Sam’s Club stores, but not competitors. Note that this doesn’t apply to items marked down or on clearance. Update, November 9th: Updated to reflect current retailer policies.

items.title: Here’s when the Black Friday sales start at Walmart, Target, and other retailers
items.author: Sheena Vasani
items.content: Black Friday officially kicks off on November 27th, but if you plan to make that the only day you buy gifts this holiday season, you’re missing out. Several prominent retailers, including Best Buy and Walmart, are preparing to roll out their holiday discounts both in-store and online. Best Buy is even offering price protection through the holiday shopping season on select goods, so if you buy early and the same item drops in price, you can get the better deal retroactively. That being said, it’s important to know how every major retailer is handling the shopping event this year, whether you plan to take advantage of the slew of early holiday deals or hold off until the day after Thanksgiving. If you plan to spend some cash, here are the schedules and expectations for Amazon, Walmart, Best Buy, and all the major retailers we know of. Amazon Amazon has yet to announce its full Black Friday playbook, but the online retailer has dropped a few early deals in its so-called Holiday Shop, including steep discounts on Sony’s WH-1000XM6 headphones, the Google Pixel 11 Pro XL, and fitness trackers like the Fitbit Inspire 3. Just be aware that Amazon does not offer price matching, so price “protection” for many Amazon shoppers means buying the item at the lower price point and returning the original — which, unfortunately, is pretty wasteful. Walmart Like in previous years, Walmart plans to roll out its Black Friday deals in three distinct waves. The first runs from November 12th through November 15th, starting online at 12:01AM ET and in stores at 6AM local time. Walmart Plus members will also get early access to some deals beginning at 12:01AM ET on November 12th, with the sale opening up to everyone at 12:01AM ET on November 13th. Walmart’s official Black Friday sale then kicks off at 12:01AM on Monday, November 23rd, with Walmart Plus members once again getting early access to select deals online. Whatever “hot Deal drops” remain will then be available to non-members at 12:01AM ET on November 24th. Walmart’s in-store Black Friday sale will then kick off at 6AM local time on November 27th. The retailer’s Cyber Monday sale, meanwhile, will kick off online at 12:01AM ET on November 30th and run through December 2nd. The retailer hasn’t shared many deal specifics yet, but did offer a sneak peek in a recent press release promising discounts across a range of categories, including toys, fashion, beauty, and home goods. Best Buy Best Buy officially kicked off its Black Friday promos on October 30th, with the retailer launching its first set of doorbuster deals on Halloween. Like last year, Best Buy will drop subsequent deals every Friday in the run-up to the holidays, and those who sign up for My Best Buy Plus or My Best Buy Total will also get up to $25 in bonus rewards during select doorbuster events. As for Best Buy’s main Black Friday event, the promos are slated to begin on November 19th and run for 10 days. The retailer will then hold its Cyber Sunday and Cyber Monday sale, followed by another round of Cyber Week deals, which will run from December 1st through the 6th. Best Buy also plans to hold a Last-Minute Savings event from December 18th through the 24th, giving shoppers yet another opportunity to save on holiday gifts. Additionally, Best Buy shoppers get holiday price protection, which means that if you purchase a qualifying item and its price drops at Best Buy during the eligible holiday period, you can request a refund for the difference. The retailer is also extending its holiday return window, allowing most purchases made between October 30th and December 31st to be returned through January 15th, 2027, or January 31st for My Best Buy Plus and Total members. Target Target’s early Black Friday sale ran from November 5th through November 7th, but the retailer also announced that it will introduce new limited-time deals every weekend throughout the holiday season. In addition, Target has brought back its “Deal of the Day” promotion, offering a new deal every day from November 1st through December 24th, with a one-day preview of upcoming offers. GameStop GameStop has yet to announce its full Black Friday 2026 sale lineup, including specific discounts on games, consoles, and accessories. In prior years, the retailer has opened as early as 7AM local time on Black Friday, though the exact hours may vary by location. We’ll update this post as more details become available. Newegg Newegg is kicking off the holiday shopping season with its Black November event, offering a new round of doorbuster deals every day from November 1st through November 30th. New discounts drop daily at 12PM ET, with deals available in limited quantities while supplies last. Shoppers can also preview the following day’s offers starting at 12PM ET. Costco Costco has already kicked off its Black Friday sale, with deals rolling out in two waves: October 30th through November 15th and November 16th through the 30th. The wholesale retailer will also offer online deals on Thanksgiving Day (Costco stores will be closed on the holiday itself), followed by a larger Black Friday sale, which runs from November 27th through the 30th. A separate, online-only Cyber Monday event will take place on November 30th. Update, November 9th: Added new details for Walmart, Best Buy, and other retailers for the 2026 shopping season.

The Jensen Huang Honeypot Fallout: What Happens Next
items.author: Alex Kantrowitz
items.content: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, head of the world’s second largest company and the backbone of the AI buildout, has admitted to an affair with a woman that U.S. intelligence believes is a Chinese spy. His board is unsure whether Nvidia‘s or U.S. state secrets were compromised, and has opened an investigation. In an AI story filled with twists and turns, this could be the biggest bombshell yet. Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has run it for 33 years, is as close to a single point of failure at Nvidia as any CEO is to any company. He has 60 direct reports, has led the firm since its inception, and has built a close relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump as pressure to limit export of his chips to China has intensified. Huang remains Nvidia CEO for now, but his ability to keep the seat may depend on what the board finds. Here’s a look at some key points in the scandal and what might happen next: This isn’t a “simple affair” On Sunday, November 8, Huang sent an email to Nvidia employees saying, “I owe my family and all of you an apology.” He had been unfaithful to his wife, he said, acknowledging that his family, colleagues, and shareholders deserve better. Some, including Pershing Square’s Bill Ackman, said they hoped (or believed) it was a “simple affair,” but it’s not that. Beyond the affair, the real issue is that Huang’s love interest, ex-Megaspeed International executive Alice Huang, is someone the United States government believes passed information to the Chinese government while building data centers with Nvidia’s help in Asia. There’s simply no getting away from this detail. This isn’t just an affair, it’s a corporate and national security issue. The unseen risks Nvidia’s board said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised” but there are ways sensitive information could have been exposed without Huang’s intent or knowledge. “Was she ever alone with his phone or computer, say when he got up to use the bathroom?” asked Sinocism writer . Huang recently took a phone call from President Trump mid-panel at a conference. There could’ve been texts or emails with the president that would’ve been of interest to Chinese intelligence. The real damage from the affair could’ve been done via sloppiness vs. explicit leaks. Nvidia’s policy credibility takes a major hit Huang had been the loudest (and most effective) voice in the U.S. lobbying against export controls of semiconductors to China. And he’s gotten a lot of what he wanted. Late last year, for instance, the Trump administration approved the sale of Nvidia’s H200 chips to China (despite the risks). Now, Huang will have little credibility in the debate, and the incident could lead to stricter export controls being put into place, impeding Nvidia’s business. Huang also denied the affair publicly, initially saying there was nothing “unusual or unexpected” about the relationship. The lying will stick with him for a while. China: An own goal? One of the more mystifying aspects of this story is why China would set a honeypot for Huang, given that he was the most effective advocate for selling AI chips to China in the U.S. Some have hypothesized that Huang became such an advocate because he was compromised. The more likely scenario is China saw it as a win either way: Don’t get caught and you potentially get key information about U.S. semiconductor plans. Get caught and the backbone of the U.S. AI industry is thrown into crisis. They got the latter. China denies the allegations. The Winners: Dario and Google Nvidia’s turmoil will be an opportunity for Anthropic and Google. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has been calling for export controls to China for years, putting him at odds with Huang. Now, Amodei will be able to advocate for his agenda with less resistance. Google, which sells TPU chips that compete with Nvidia’s GPUs, also has a window to capitalize on its competitor’s woes. Google today announced two new TPU variants, with one built especially for work in governments and highly regulated industries. Good timing. Story continues below… Perplexity’s Personal CFO is powered by Plaid (sponsor) Asking people to connect their financial accounts requires trust. That’s why Perplexity built Personal CFO on Plaid. Hear Jeff Grimes, Head of Capabilities Product at Perplexity, break down how Plaid’s broad account coverage and permissioned data access helps them deliver more personalized guidance. Read the full story Continued from above.. What’s next for Jensen: Hearings in Washington The timing could not be worse for Huang, whose scandal arrives at the exact moment anti-AI Democrats are about to take power in Congress. Artificial intelligence is unpopular in the United States and was bound to be the subject of hearings. Now, the newly empowered Dems could have their first target: A high-profile, close friend of Trump who stepped into the wrong honeypot. Staffers are probably already salivating at the clips their bosses will generate for X and YouTube. Will Jensen stay on as Nvidia CEO? Read more

items.title: F1 in Brazil: You’ve got to keep your tires alive
items.author: Jonathan M. Gitlin
items.content: In sports, a “dead rubber” is a match that takes place after the outcome of the series or championship has already been decided. The people in charge hate this*—if you wrap up a title two-thirds of the way through a season, the viewers evaporate, as there’s nothing left at stake. But anyone who decided to skip this year’s Brazilian Grand Prix this past weekend missed one of the year’s most entertaining races, as a combination of a mixed-up starting order, some very fast drivers at the back, and a wet track that dried and then saw rain again resulted in action aplenty. A peculiarity of F1 is that even if you manage to win a championship, there’s no guarantee you’ll be in a position to defend it. Take McLaren’s Lando Norris, who took the crown in 2025 after a nail-biting fight with his teammate Oscar Piastri and Red Bull’s Max Verstappen. Sadly for Lando, McLaren did not start this year in a position to win races, and even with several upgrades, the team has produced a car that is still very tricky to drive. But this weekend in Brazil, Norris demonstrated the form that earned him the number 1. Rain on Saturday during qualifying helped jumble the usual running order. It was heavy enough that drivers used the wet weather tire with deep treads, which usually generates so much spray that visibility disappears and running has to be suspended. But with fewer cars on track in the later knockout qualifying sessions, this was not a problem for once. More disruption came from grid penalties for Verstappen and Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton, both of whom needed to use extra power unit components outside of the season’s allowance.
