items.title: Extending LLDB to Debug Applications That Span CPUs and GPUs
items.content: We built a vendor-neutral accelerator plugin architecture in lldb-server for debugging applications that span CPUs and GPUs. It separates shared debugger infrastructure from hardware-specific device control. The design represents the CPU and GPU as separate debugger processes while presenting them in one debugging session. Modern AI applications rarely execute in one place. A workload can begin in a high-level framework and move back and forth between native CPU code and kernels running on a GPU. When a bug crosses those boundaries, developers need to understand the host application and the device together. That is harder than attaching a conventional debugger to another process. The CPU and GPU may use different instruction sets, registers, memory spaces, and execution models. The GPU is also controlled through a runtime and driver inside the host process, so debugging the device often requires careful coordination with the CPU. Historically, GPU vendors built device-specific debuggers, including AMD’s ROCgdb and NVIDIA’s CUDA-GDB. These tools provide deep support for their respective platforms, but common debugger capabilities must often be implemented and maintained separately. At Meta, we have been developing a different approach for LLDB: a common accelerator plugin architecture in lldb-server. In this post, “GPU” refers to the concrete devices and examples, while “accelerator” refers to LLDB’s broader, vendor-neutral plugin abstraction. The architecture has evolved through contributions from engineers at Meta and across the accelerator ecosystem. It keeps the shared debugger independent of any one GPU while giving hardware vendors a focused place to implement device-specific behavior. Why GPU Debugging Challenges Traditional Debugger Models A traditional debugger generally assumes that one process has one architecture and a consistent view of threads, registers, and memory. GPU programs challenge each of those assumptions. A host process might run on x86-64 while its kernels use a completely different instruction set. A CPU thread has a familiar register context, while a GPU may execute groups of lanes in lockstep. Host and device pointers can refer to different address spaces. A GPU can expose thousands of execution lanes, which do not map cleanly onto the thread model that most command-line and graphical debuggers present. Combining all of this state into one artificial process model makes the debugger more complicated. Every operation must first determine whether it applies to the CPU or the GPU. Register handling, memory reads, breakpoints, stepping, and stop events all become conditional on the selected hardware. A single process model also forces the CPU and GPU into one unified memory map, even though their address spaces can be independent: The same address, such as 0x1000, can refer to different locations in the CPU and GPU processes. Instead of hiding those differences, the LLDB accelerator architecture gives them a clear boundary. Plugin Support in lldb-server for GPU Debugging LLDB uses a companion process called lldb-server to launch or attach to a program and perform low-level debugging operations. The LLDB client communicates with the server through the GDB remote protocol, a command protocol for operations such as reading memory, inspecting registers, controlling execution, and setting breakpoints. Because lldb-server already controls the native process, it is also the right place to coordinate with an accelerator runtime. The new plugin interface lets a hardware-specific backend work alongside the normal CPU debugger. The backend translates a vendor’s device debugging API into concepts LLDB already understands, such as processes, threads, registers, memory, modules, and stop reasons. This separation keeps the LLDB client vendor-neutral. Common improvements to the command line, remote protocol, symbol handling, and IDE integration can benefit every accelerator. At the same time, each vendor remains responsible for the details that are unique to its hardware and driver stack. GPU debugging support is activated only when the debugged application uses a supported GPU runtime. For CPU-only applications, LLDB and lldb-server continue through the existing native debugging path without incurring runtime computational overhead. Two Targets, One Debugging Experience The architecture represents the CPU and accelerator as separate LLDB targets. Each target has its own architecture and is associated with a debugger process that maintains its threads, registers, address space, and execution state. The CPU continues to use LLDB’s established native debugging path. When the accelerator becomes available, the plugin provides a second connection that LLDB uses to create the device target. To the debugger, the two targets remain technically independent. To the developer, they can appear in one LLDB or IDE session. This avoids forcing incompatible CPU and GPU concepts into a single process while still supporting a unified workflow. The CPU and GPU remain separate LLDB targets while a plugin in lldb-server coordinates host and device debugging. Coordinating the Host and Device A typical debugging session follows a small set of steps: LLDB connects to lldb-server and discovers which accelerator plugins are available. A plugin can ask LLDB to set internal breakpoints in the host process. These breakpoints identify important runtime events, such as the point at which a GPU debugging session can begin. When the host reaches one of those points, lldb-server notifies the plugin. The plugin initializes the vendor debugging API and prepares an accelerator debugging endpoint. LLDB creates a second target for the accelerator and connects to it. Device threads, registers, memory, modules, and breakpoints can then use LLDB’s existing abstractions. Structured actions coordinate the two sides. A plugin can request CPU breakpoints, provide connection information, report device modules, and synchronize host and device execution. The common protocol describes what the debugger needs to do without exposing vendor-specific API details to the LLDB client. We also built a mock accelerator plugin that exercises this flow without specialized hardware. It lets the LLVM test suite verify discovery, breakpoint coordination, connection creation, and basic device state. This has been important for developing shared infrastructure that can be reviewed and tested independently of any particular GPU. A Typical GPU Workflow The vector dot-product HIP sample produced this abridged session: (lldb) target list Current targets: target #0: gpu_demo (x86_64, stopped) * target #1: amd_memory_kernel[...] (amdgcn, stopped) (lldb) b compute_element Breakpoint 1: no locations (pending). (lldb) c (lldb) target select 0 (lldb) c Launching kernel: 2 blocks x 32 threads 1 location added to breakpoint 1 Target 1 stopped. (lldb) target select 1 (lldb) bt * frame #0: compute_element(..., idx=32) at gpu_demo.hip:26 frame #1: vector_dot_kernel(..., n=64) at gpu_demo.hip:35 The pending breakpoint resolves when the GPU module loads, and the backtrace comes from the GPU target. A Common Plugin Framework Across Hardware Vendors The plugin boundary is intentionally based on debugger operations rather than concepts from a specific GPU platform. That makes it useful across devices with very different instruction sets, runtime APIs, and execution models. The framework supports postmortem GPU debugging as well as live sessions. GPU core-dump plugins use a common base class for their LLDB integration, while vendor implementations provide the device-specific thread, register, memory, and module state. GPU debugging efforts at Meta are already leveraging the architecture. Because we operate a heterogeneous fleet of GPUs with different hardware and software stacks, the fact that these efforts use the same model is an important validation of the design: the common LLDB layer can remain stable while each backend represents its own device accurately. At the time of writing, we have upstreamed most of the common framework to LLVM. This includes the lldb-server plugin interface; GDB-remote packets for plugin discovery, initialization, runtime-event coordination, and GPU connection creation; support for associating CPU and GPU debugger processes while preserving their independent architecture; support for multiple address spaces, and hardware-independent mock tests. We expect to upstream the remaining pieces soon. Looking Ahead Next, we plan to finish upstreaming the remaining common infrastructure and expand the vendor integrations built on it. Our goal is that integrating new hardware with LLDB should require only a vendor-specific plugin, not a separate debugger to build and maintain. Acknowledgements We are grateful to Meta’s Developer Infrastructure leadership team, especially Shane Nay, Todd Fiala, and Ale Contenti, whose direct support made this work possible. We also thank our Debugging & Tooling teammates Jacob Lalonde, David Young, Alexandre Perez, Zhiyuan Li, Piyush Jaiswal, and Philip DePetro for their collaboration and support. Finally, we thank the open source community, especially Jonas Devlieghere, Jim Ingham, David Spickett, and Jason Molenda, for reviewing the RFCs and upstream pull requests. The post Extending LLDB to Debug Applications That Span CPUs and GPUs appeared first on Engineering at Meta.

items.title: Fact-Checking at Scale: Building a More Accurate and Efficient Synopsis Factuality System
items.author: Netflix Technology Blog
items.content: By Shreya S Ramanujam, Yongce Li, Afshine Amidi, Sina Ghiassian, Benjamin Klein. Introduction Picture this — you’re home after a long day at work and can’t wait to catch up on Bridgerton. You log on to Netflix, search for “Bridgerton” and land on this screen: If this sounds familiar, you already know what a synopsis is — it’s a short glimpse into what a viewer can expect to see in a show. We see two types of synopses here: a series-level synopsis describing the overarching plot, and multiple episode-level synopses describing each episode. A synopsis plays a very important role for us — it helps viewers decide whether a title is worth watching or not. Every synopsis needs to strike a balance: sharing just enough to give viewers a sense of what to expect, while leaving enough intrigue to draw them in. But of course, we can’t just write anything. “In the fog-drenched streets of Victorian London, Detective Daphne Bridgerton races to unmask a serial killer known only as the elusive Lady Whistledown.” Intriguing? Definitely. But it is most certainly not the premise of Bridgerton. Which leads us to the first (and most important) rule of writing a good synopsis: it must be factual. At Netflix’s scale, with thousands of titles, multiple episodes per season and multiple languages, fact-checking all of these by hand simply doesn’t scale. This is where our factuality service comes in: an automated way to judge whether a synopsis is factual or not. Our current factuality checker feeds a reasoning model everything we know about a title (like metadata and text assets) and asks it to judge synopsis factuality according to a rigorous rubric. There are two main limitations of this approach that we want to optimize: High cost of long-context reasoning calls: Each decision requires expensive, long-context model calls to reasoning models, which doesn’t scale well when we want to check multiple titles, episodes, languages, and style variants. Misaligned rationales: The model’s explanations often diverge from our annotators’ reasoning, which makes its factuality verdicts less reliable. We want these rationales to be better aligned so that (1) the model can consistently flag nuanced errors, and (2) its explanations can be used downstream to automatically correct issues in the synopsis. Our new approach tackles both problems at once. On the cost side, it delivers a 52.4% reduction per synopsis. On the quality side, it significantly improves both verdict accuracy and reasoning alignment: Recall–Fail (“Of all truly non-factual synopses, how many does the system correctly reject?”) rises from 0.77 to 0.86, and the new factuality service’s explanations now show ~82% overlap with human rationales (up from ~69%). In other words, it’s not just cheaper and more accurate — it’s also much better aligned with how our expert annotators actually judge synopses. So, what exactly does factuality mean? Let’s go back to the Bridgerton example. Say you see this synopsis about Bridgerton Season 1: Synopsis A: “Bridgerton follows Daphne Bridgerton, the eldest daughter of the powerful Bridgerton family as she makes her debut onto Regency London’s competitive marriage market.” It’s easy to judge that this synopsis is factually correct — no wrong facts, and it gives the reader a clear, accurate glimpse of what to expect from the show. Let’s take another example: Synopsis B: “Set in modern-day London, this gritty crime drama follows Detective Daphne Bridgerton as she hunts a serial killer while hiding her own criminal past.” Another easy one — the plot is so blatantly off the mark that it is definitely not factual. But what about this? Synopsis C: “Bridgerton follows the mysterious, sharp-tongued Lady Whistledown as she exposes the secrets of London’s high society through her scandalous gossip sheet.” Technically, every statement here is true — Lady Whistledown does indeed publish a gossip sheet, and if there’s one thing she is known for, it’s her scathing exposés. So then, is this a factual synopsis? Not quite! While technically true, it paints a misleading picture of the show. A new viewer might reasonably expect it to revolve around Lady Whistledown, rather than Daphne navigating the marriage market. This, too, is a type of non-factuality we want to catch. Lastly, here’s the trickiest of all: Synopsis D: “When Daphne Bridgerton makes her society debut, she catches the eye of the aloof Duke of Hastings, and the two begin a passionate love affair that sets the whole ton abuzz.” Again, every statement is true, but the phrasing is misleading. A new viewer might assume they fall in love immediately, missing the fact that their relationship begins as a fake, mutually beneficial arrangement. This is another type of nuanced error our system should flag. So now that we have an idea of the kinds of errors we care about, the real question is: how do we build a system that is able to catch both glaring as well as subtle factuality violations? Current Service and Its Limitations Our current factuality pipeline is a straightforward, holistic LLM call. We feed a reasoning model everything we know about a title (text assets, metadata, and a detailed factuality rubric) and ask it to judge the factuality of a synopsis. We repeat the call several times to reduce output randomness, and if any run flags the synopsis as non-factual, it fails. This approach has two main limitations: High cost: Each judgment requires multiple (five, to be exact) calls to a large reasoning model over extremely long contexts (100k+ tokens), which does not scale well. Misaligned reasoning: The model can fail synopses for nitpicky reasons (e.g., “This is a show about wonderful magic” gets failed because the characters never literally call the magic “wonderful”) while overlooking nuanced errors by convincing itself they “don’t really make the synopsis false.” This misalignment makes verdicts less reliable and rationales less useful for downstream correction. Optimizing the Holistic Pipeline To understand exactly where we should optimize the current holistic pipeline, we study the current pipeline both qualitatively and quantitatively on a custom factuality benchmark that we built. This benchmark comprises synopses hand-labeled by human annotators as factual or non-factual, along with their rationales. This analysis reveals several key insights: Insight 1: Do we really need five holistic calls? Let’s think back to why we added multiple holistic calls in the first place: to reduce sampling noise. In practice, though, we see an interesting dichotomy: Blatantly true / false synopses (Bridgerton A, B): All runs agree on the verdict with near-identical reasoning. Nuanced errors (Bridgerton C, D): The model is much more likely to disagree with itself — some runs catch the error, some don’t. This is exactly where additional sampling helps. This suggests a simple optimization: A and B don’t really need all 5 calls. If we can somehow identify these “easy” synopses upfront, we can cut down on the number of calls for them, while still giving harder cases like C and D the extra calls they need. The easiest way to do this is to ask the model to output its confidence alongside its verdict and rationale. We can then separate “easy” (high confidence) synopses from “hard” (low confidence) ones and only send the hard cases through additional checks. Think of it like airport security: most bags go straight through, but those that trigger the alarm (low confidence) get extra screening. Implementing this easy fix makes our pipeline go from the current holistic model to a new “confidence gated” holistic model: Insight 2: Five identical judges calls give us no new information With confidence gating, our pipeline only escalates harder synopses to the full five holistic calls. But extra calls only help with sampling noise, not systematic reasoning errors: if every run follows the same flawed rationale, they’ll all reach the same wrong verdict, rendering the extra calls useless. How can we ensure that each call counts? Idea: Diversify the judges and make them specialized Instead of running five holistic judges with the same generic factuality prompt, we introduce two specialized judges that individually target the two aspects of factuality we care about: Literal Judge: Is the synopsis literally true? Implicature Judge: Does this synopsis give a false picture to a new reader who has not watched this show? Explicitly searching for specific types of errors helps us better flag both literal and subtler implicature errors. In practice, we observe that this works better than repeatedly querying a single holistic judge, hoping that sampling stochasticity will surface nuanced errors. Insight 3: The rationale reveals mistakes the verdict hid At this point, we have a pretty good pipeline, but we’re still underusing one of the richest signals available to us: the model’s rationale behind its verdict. For nuanced errors, we often see the model identify a point of contention, then brush it aside based on a faulty assumption or because it deems the issue too minor to affect the verdict. Can we use these shaky spots in the rationale to catch (and correct) errors the verdict misses? Idea: Secondary atomic-claim checking via a router: Since our literal and implicature judges are already strong reasoning models, we ask them to additionally critically analyse their own reasoning and surface shaky spots — any doubts, concessions, or assumptions that might need rechecking. These include cases where the model: Makes an assumption. Raises a doubt that the available evidence can’t resolve (e.g., an external critic quote). Notices a contradiction but dismisses it as insufficient to change the verdict. We pass all concessions from both judges to a router model, which: Reframes them as self-contained, verifiable atomic claims, each with a materiality field specifying the evidence needed to support or refute it. Routes each claim to the appropriate secondary Stage-2 judge: a web judge for external facts (e.g., citations, media quotes, or prior work), or a source-material recheck focused on the reframed atomic claim. By pinpointing the exact point of contention, the recheck is more targeted, making it easier to mark the claim as true or false. Putting It All Together: Proposed Cascade Factuality Service Our findings lead to three key improvements: specialized judges, confidence-gated escalation, and targeted rechecking of shaky reasoning using a secondary stage when escalated. We implement these improvements as a tiered system shown in the figure below: every synopsis first passes through both the literal and the implicature judges. High-confidence verdicts are retained, while low-confidence cases escalate to the router and Stage-2 judges for further checking. Stage 2 can overturn the initial verdict in two cases: FAIL → PASS: All concessions, including the original failure reasons, are supported by the secondary check. PASS → FAIL: At least one concession is contradicted. Results Based on our discussions from above, we evaluate three different pipelines: Evaluation: Datasets and Metrics We evaluate these systems on two datasets: show-level and episode-level synopses. Each datapoint includes a synopsis, a human gold label (factual / not factual), and the annotator’s rationale. For episode-level synopses, we additionally require that the synopsis be specific to that particular episode, not just a generic synopsis of the overall show. We focus on two main axes: Quality and Cost. The quality metrics are listed below: Recall-FAIL is our primary metric: higher recall means fewer Gold FAILs are missed. We also track Precision-PASS, which measures how reliably PASS verdicts identify Gold PASSes, and alignment with human rationales. On the cost side, we want to reduce both the average number of LLM calls per synopsis and the end-to-end cost of producing a final verdict. Latency is not our primary optimization target, but we do want to ensure the median (P50) latency does not blow up to impractical judgement times. Evaluation Results The best numbers per metric per dataset are shown in bold. Note: We compared the cascade against two holistic ablations — increased reasoning effort and a smaller, cheaper model — to test if simple ablations could achieve better performance. For episode-level synopses, we also added a full-show summary to the prompt to provide context from previous episodes; we observe summaries substantially improve performance when compared to non-summary context variants, so we report only summary-based variants. Our takeaways from this experiment are: Cascade improves quality. Our primary metric, Recall-FAIL improves on both show and episode level synopses, with a limited impact on Recall-PASS. In other words, we now catch more Gold FAIL synopses without sacrificing the reliability of our PASS verdicts. Cascade is cheaper. Cascade cuts total cost by 52.4% on the show-level dataset. Cascade (with summary) is also 15% cheaper than the current (no summary) holistic pipeline on episodic dataset. Cascade’s P50 latency increases with respect to the holistic baseline. Even so, this remains within what we consider a reasonable range for factuality judgment. Simple tweaks aren’t enough. Increasing reasoning effort makes the factuality checker too lenient, while using a smaller model makes it too strict — neither addresses the underlying problems of the holistic baseline. Summary context matters for episodic tasks. Without a full-show summary, the model tends to over-fail because it lacks the context to determine whether a detail from the episode summary fits the broader storyline. Alignment with Human Rationale So far, we’ve established that the cascade produces better verdicts: it catches more non-factual synopses and produces more reliable PASS decisions. But are these verdicts correct for the right reasons? To measure this, we use an LLM-as-a-Judge to compare each pipeline’s reasoning against the human rationale on Gold-FAIL (GF) synopses. The judge assigns a Reasoning Similarity Score (RSS) of 0 (dissimilar), 0.5 (partially similar), or 1 (very similar) based on rationale overlap. We observe that cascade is significantly better aligned with human rationale in all cases. This is a big gain — not only is the cascade giving us more accurate factuality verdicts, but it also identifies the same points of contention in the synopsis as a specialized human annotator. Conclusion + Future Work Overall, our proposed cascade pipeline improves both cost and quality of the existing factuality service: On the cost side, confidence gating lets us avoid unnecessary calls, reducing the average cost of factuality evaluation. On the quality side, two diverse judges allow us to collect complementary informative verdicts, while the Stage-2 judges recheck and correct the assumptions behind uncertain decisions. This results in higher verdict accuracy and substantially better alignment between model and expert annotator reasoning. The cascade gives us a path toward a factuality system that is not just more accurate, but also more interpretable and self-correcting. Some future directions to consider would be: Adding multimodal inputs to help verify claims that text assets alone cannot confirm. Use the rationale from factuality checking to correct the faulty synopsis. Fact-Checking at Scale: Building a More Accurate and Efficient Synopsis Factuality System was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.title: What Frontier Labs Buy: A Data Deep Dive with Handshake AI — Garrett Lord & Team
items.author: swyx .ai
items.content: This is our first Latent Space deep dive with an AI data company. In roughly a year, Handshake’s AI training business went from launch to $1 billion in gross annualized revenue. What are frontier labs buying at that scale? What evals are models still nowhere close to human level on? Garrett Lord brought the people who build these reinforcement learning environments to show us. For the first time, we are walking through them live! To cover the scope of Handshake, we had to produce a very special joint podcast across our Science/Engineering/Research/Finance podcast hosts, because Handshake’s business runs across all these and more. Watch for three segments after the general intro: Finance. In the finance demo, the agent has to find its assignment in a bank’s email, work out which files govern the deal, and deliver a workbook. Watch what happens to one line in the client’s email about existing goodwill. The agent carries the number into Python and subtracts it. Collin points out that the model can explain the tax treatment when you ask it directly. The mistake comes when it has to recognize that this particular line of code is where the rule applies. Bio. Nick Magazine and Jonas Mueller show us VIALS, Handshake’s benchmark for interpreting the images scientists use at work. Nick puts nine slides of brain-tumor tissue on screen and asks which two show the most advanced vessel necrosis. Give yourself a moment before his answer. Nick picks H and I. The model picks those two and adds G. Watching Nick point to what’s missing from the tissue is more instructive than seeing the score. Coding. In a simulated file-access task, the team can inspect which files an agent read, whether it checked the copies, and what it did to the shell history afterward. A transcript of the agent’s final reply would miss most of what Steve Kelling and Nishant Ranka are evaluating. Who’s in the room 🟣 AI data business — Garrett Lord, Sahil Bhaiwala and Nishant Ranka open and close the episode on the market for expert data. 🌸 Life sciences — Nick Magazine and Jonas Mueller put the gel and brain-tissue tasks on screen. 🟢 Finance — Collin Schweiker and Sahil Bhaiwala take us through Project Falcon and its Excel grader. 🟠 Alignment — Steve Kelling and Nishant Ranka follow the agent’s tool calls through the safety simulations. Show notes ATLAS-Finance — Explore the benchmark for agents working across a simulated bank’s inboxes, documents, and financial models. Inside a bank — Handshake traces a separate published deal, Project Osprey, from the client’s email to a grading decision. The deal on screen in our interview is Project Falcon. VIALS sample tasks — Try the scientific image questions, including the gel and brain-tissue tasks from the episode. How Handshake trained a model to read scientific figures — The team describes using intermediate image descriptions to train and evaluate a vision-language model.
